title: How MCA Debt Relief Works: Options, Costs, and Written Agreements
excerpt: A practical MCA workout process: identify the product, assess cash flow, request available adjustments, compare proposals, and document any agreed resolution.
author: Business Debt Insider
contentMd:
MCA debt relief can mean a payment adjustment, a negotiated settlement, a restructure, or help evaluating legal and insolvency options. These approaches have different costs and consequences. Hiring a consulting firm does not automatically change an agreement, stop withdrawals, or require a funder to accept a proposal.

**Editorial correction — October 11, 2026:** We removed unsupported savings ranges, standard completion timelines, and claims that reconciliation guarantees a pause. The steps below are a planning framework, not a promise of a particular outcome.

## 1. Identify every obligation

Create a list of each financing company, the legal counterparty, product, amount received, fees, scheduled payments, claimed balance, and any past-due amounts. A loan and a purchase of future receivables can both have frequent withdrawals; payment frequency does not identify the product.

Collect signed agreements, amendments, payment authorizations, bank statements, payoff statements, relevant UCC records, guarantees, and legal notices. Separate what the creditor claims from what your records confirm. The [lender directory](/lenders) links to published product information, but your agreement controls the terms of your account.

## 2. Build a cash-flow picture

List expected receipts and essential operating expenses before deciding what a proposed arrangement could sustain. Include taxes, payroll, rent, insurance, and payments to creditors outside the proposed program. Test a weaker-revenue scenario as well as the expected one.

A lower daily debit is not necessarily a lower total cost. Compare the amount owed before and after a proposal, its duration, new fees, and any new security or guarantees. Our [stack calculator](/tools/stack-calculator) helps organize scheduled payments, while the [APR calculator](/tools/apr-calculator) estimates annualized cost for a stated equal-payment schedule. Neither determines legal enforceability or an affordable payment for your particular business.

## 3. Check available servicing options

Read the adjustment or reconciliation provision, if any, and request the documents the servicer requires. Keep a copy of the request and ask for written confirmation of the response and effective date.

[Forward Financing's published revenue-based contract highlights](https://www.forwardfinancing.com/resources/forward-revenue-based-financing-contract-highlights/) illustrate that payment adjustments and reconciliation may be distinct processes. That example cannot be applied automatically to a different agreement or a loan. Sending a request does not itself establish permission to reduce or stop a debit.

If a withdrawal appears unauthorized or inconsistent with an agreement, contact your bank promptly. For more detail, read the [business ACH guide](/insights/stop-mca-daily-ach-debits).

## 4. Compare the proposed paths

| Path | What may change | What to establish before relying on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contractual reconciliation or adjustment | Collection amount or timing under the agreement | Eligibility, required documents, calculation, and effective date |
| Negotiated restructure | Payment schedule or other agreed terms | Total payback, fees, maturity, and consequences of a missed revised payment |
| Negotiated settlement | Resolution for an agreed amount or schedule | Written creditor acceptance, releases, covered parties, and completion conditions |
| New financing | Cash available and creditor mix | Net proceeds, old balances actually discharged, new cost, and affordability |
| Legal or insolvency review | Available defenses or formal procedures | Advice from appropriately licensed counsel based on the facts |

A creditor can reject a proposal. An agreement with one creditor does not resolve the others. Where litigation, guarantees, or disputed contract terms are involved, clarify which lawyer is responsible and whether there is a separate engagement and fee.

## 5. Evaluate the service provider and full cost

Ask for a written scope explaining who does the work, how fees are earned, when they are charged, and what happens if no creditor accepts an offer. Identify exclusions such as litigation, tax advice, appeals, or additional negotiations.

If money is held in a program account, ask who owns and controls the account, who receives statements, when funds can be withdrawn, and what cancellation entails. Do not assume every program uses escrow or that depositing money into an account satisfies creditor obligations.

Compare total creditor payments plus provider, legal, and account fees against a clearly defined starting balance. Keep proposed savings separate from completed results. Our [settlement evidence guide](/insights/mca-settlement-success-rates) explains why a headline discount is not the same as net savings.

The [FTC's small-business financing guidance](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/blog/2020/08/protecting-small-businesses-seeking-financing-during-pandemic) discusses deceptive financing practices and the need for accurate information. A provider's marketing claim should be checked against its written terms and supporting evidence.

## 6. Document acceptance and follow through

Before relying on a change, obtain the signed agreement or other written acceptance required for that arrangement. Confirm the creditor and accounts covered, payment dates, treatment of fees, default terms, and what releases or termination documents will be provided after completion.

Track each payment and keep proof of receipt. Request confirmation when the agreed conditions are satisfied. Do not assume paying an amount automatically removes every lien or releases a guarantor: check the relevant documents and applicable procedures with counsel.

Canceled debt can have tax consequences, subject to exceptions and exclusions. The [IRS's canceled-debt guidance](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc431) is a starting point; an accountant should assess your situation.

## How long does a program take?

There is no completion time established by this guide. Document availability, available funds, creditor decisions, proposed schedules, and legal proceedings can all affect timing. Ask for a plan that identifies dependencies and review dates, together with what happens if a proposed milestone is missed.

BDI has not established a verified industry-wide savings or completion-rate dataset. Any example should identify whether it is hypothetical or a documented case, and a past case does not establish the result of a new one.

## Prepare for an initial review

Bring your creditor list, contracts, recent financial records, and any notices with deadlines. Write down the maximum outflow the business can sustain under your cash-flow scenarios. [Contact BDI](/contact) to organize the financial review, and seek independent legal advice for legal questions. BDI is a financial consulting business, not a law firm.
